rv.q: It's a surprisingly moving experience that make you feel that though you're watching separate lives of these strangers on a train, you're hearing the heart of one connected urban village.
More to the point, In Transit, while boasting engaging performances, features cliched characters and situations too bland for a sitcom, let alone theater.
Acknowledging this is rather like admiring the ingenuity that must have gone into a sentimental picture of a rainbow, perhaps with the Care Bears in the foreground, rendered entirely in bottle caps.
Sanitized subway musical with a capella harmonies.
The rest of us will grow tired of numbers that sound like ’70s sitcom theme songs or advertising jingles.

The bigger problem with the new musical In Transit, which opened tonight at Circle in the Square, is that it randomly jams the two gimmicks together and, lacking a more meaningful animating principle, promptly derails.
The pop-song score is so watery and texturally unvaried that the initial charm of seeing an a cappella show wears off long before 'In Transit' winds to a close
A joyful, heartfelt, complicated celebration of New York City that will appeal to most tourists and jaded locals like myself.
It can still touch us, make us laugh, make us reflect, and most interestingly, have something on its mind about the human condition.
The show's creators have crafted something genuinely fresh and exuberant, a musical that celebrates the diversity and resilience of urban life without condescending to its characters or audience.
“In Transit” manages to create a reality-distortion field that left me feeling the MTA isn’t the hostile environment I know it all too well to be.
Leave your cynicism on the other side of the turnstile and swipe yourself in.
That's a sweet thought, and this is a sweet, earnest musical.
In Transit arrives at its Broadway station safely and soundly, but misses the emotional connection needed to make it an express hit.
Unfortunately, the freshness of the voice-only orchestra doesn’t completely compensate for the flat familiarity of much else in the musical.
In Transit attempts to dramatize that sense of awe and wonderment into a full-length musical with bland results.
As for In Transit here and now, the use of a cappella is hardly enough to float the show; but without the a cappella distinction, would anyone today have bothered to bring this musical to Broadway?
And while the cast is sprightly and talented, the issues their characters face are way too familiar to be interesting.
In Transit is a musical that's easier to admire than to love, though it certainly deserves credit for its ambition and its performers' considerable talents.
If only their vehicle didn’t feel as if it was stalled between stations.
Whether above ground or below ground, the “In Transit” characters lead one to re-title the show “Theaters Are for Sleeping.”
The show (which has music, lyrics and book from four different writers) is well-meant, but the premise is corny and the characters are generic.
But the novelty of vocally supplied accompaniment to the songs comes with its own shortcomings.
A show packed tighter with clichés than a rush-hour train with straphangers.
In Transit puts it all together to create one of the most creative and enjoyable musicals on Broadway.
It’s a harmonious fun journey with this group of commuters, one that I would trade in for any day of the week.

Because every member of the cast is charming, the songs utterly infectious, and every single time they open their mouths to spin their glorious harmonies you completely forget how many times before you've heard all those theatrical tropes.
The energetic and talented company made the show a joy to watch.
This incarnation of the show is zippy, toe-tapping, touching, and upbeat with a heartwarming message.
The New York insider jokes and incredible vocal prowess make it an enjoyable ride.
Where it lacks in thematic profundity, the show shines with its humor, delivering a charming and witty love letter to life in the city.
Generally this is a slick and likeable excursion that advocates enjoying the ride.
One's opinion of this show will depend largely on their fondness for a cappella music

Despite the heroic effort of the creators to spin a musical tale that connects deeply with urban dwellers and their current challenging exigencies, the musical remains formulaic and less than distinguished.
Trite is the term that leaps immediately to mind, and it’s hard to shake.
I’m sorry, I just can’t get into a show where the biggest number is about selling out.
As if we haven’t been disappointed enough earlier this year–what a way to end the 2016. Broadway season on another sad note indeed.

cn.t: Critics are mixed on Broadway's first a cappella musical, praising the impressive vocal harmonies and talented cast but finding the subway-set story clichéd and thin, with stock characters on predictable journeys.

sg.ra: In the 3/4 thrust configuration these front rows put you at the lip of the playing area with actors entering from aisles directly beside you. Headout notes rows AA-B are 'closest to the stage' and audiences are 'roped into the play's action.' Because the stage is surrounded on three sides, the acting is deliberately blocked so no front row gets a sustained back-of-actor view, but individual moments will face away from you — that is inherent to in-the-round and not a flaw of this section.

Universally cited as the optimal vantage in this thrust venue — close enough to feel the intimacy of a 776-seat room with only 10 rows, but one row back from the front so sightlines catch the whole three-sided playing area. Headout: 'Center Orchestra - rows B, C and D' positioned centrally are 'possibly the best seats in the house.' The in-the-round blocking is designed so these central rows at eye-level with the floor see choreography and staging as intended.

Because the venue only has 10 rows total and stadium-inclined seating, rows H-I still feel close to the thrust while giving elevated sightlines that reveal staging patterns on the floor — useful for musicals with choreography. Headout: 'Rows H and I in the upper middle level offer a great view of the stage and the prices are lower than those of the premium orchestra seats.' AVFMS reviewer MusicaltheatreWhiz in H144 (Just in Time, Feb 2026): 'There really isn't a bad seat in the house!' TripAdvisor: 'up is better for musicals.'

In a typical Broadway house the last row would be a skip, but Circle in the Square is only 10 rows deep so row K is roughly where Row G would be in a standard theater. AVFMS danielb9 at K109 (Just in Time, Feb 28 2026): 'Enough legroom to be comfortable and despite being in the back row felt very connected to the action.' Multiple reviews note 'no obstruction' and 'great seat' for row K. Stadium incline ensures sightlines over heads. The in-the-round nature means some scenes still play toward the opposite side, but this is a venue property not a section flaw.

sg.n: Side Sections - Long Arms of the Horseshoe (100s & 200s)
sg.ra: The two long 'wide sides' of the horseshoe (the 100 and 200 numbered sections per BWW forum user Patash's question about 102/202 numbering) give a profile view of the main action. TripAdvisor: 'the two wide sides are fine' and are preferred over 'straight in front' which is 'too far from the rear end of the main stage.' AVFMS samr32 at C207 (Just in Time, Feb 26 2026): 'Amazing seat! Can see both stages so well, and the actors (including Jonathan Groff) run up and down the aisle right near you.' The 300-degree blocking means side sections regularly get face-forward moments; not behind-stage.

The one sustained warning across every source is the extreme corner seats where the horseshoe's ends meet the stage. Headout/TickPick specifically: 'seats 438-440 are obstructed when actors perform on the far left of the stage and vice versa for the opposite side' (437-439). Unlike the rest of the house where in-the-round angles are temporary, these corner positions can have whole extended scenes played entirely out of view on the opposite corner. In a 3/4 thrust with actors using the full perimeter, this is a structural flaw of the seat, not a temporary blocking issue.
